title: Supercurrent-controlled spontaneous ferromagnetism of magnetic impurities in a spin-orbit-coupled superconductor

paper_content.abstract:
Conventional superconductors disfavor ferromagnetism because the supercurrent-carrying
electrons are paired into anti-parallel spin singlets. Consequently, ferromagnetic coupling
between localized moments through the charge carriers is absent in s-wave superconductors.
However, Rashba-type spin-orbit coupling (SOC) can profoundly alter the interaction between
the charge carriers and localized spins. Here, we report long-range ferromagnetic order among
the impurity moments on the surface of an s-wave SOC superconductor, Fe(Se,Te). We employ
scanning superconducting quantum interference device microscopy and find suppressed vortex
states but spontaneous magnetic domains in the superconducting state. Homogeneous remanent
flux patterns are induced by applying supercurrents through the sample. The patterns are
consistent with anomalous edge and bulk supercurrents generated by long-range in-plane
magnetization related to the magneto-electric effect intrinsic to a Rashba superconductor. The
anomalous supercurrents occur above a bias current threshold and follow hysteresis loops
reminiscent of those of a ferromagnet. Surprisingly, the magnetic switching (super)current
density is three orders of magnitude less than that in a ferromagnetic metal with SOC.
These observations suggest an emergent ferromagnetic impurity state in a Rashba superconductor,
which can be controlled by applying supercurrents.
paper_content.introduction:
One of the immediate challenges facing high-speed computation using superconductors is a lack of fast
cryogenic memory with low drive power [1]. Non-superconducting memories widely used nowadays
are too slow and power-demanding for single-flux quantum electronics [2]. Superconducting memories
based on Josephson junctions [3,4] provide a faster solution but suffer from vortex trapping and
scalability problem [5]. A magnetic superconductor which can be switched by a supercurrent may be a
candidate material to overcome these current limitations. However, extrinsic ferromagnetic moments
breaks Cooper pairs in s-wave superconductors and supercurrent exerts Lorentz force on free vortices,
causing energy dissipation.

Utilizing supercurrent to mediate ferromagnetism among local magnetic moments may overcome these
problems. In normal metals, charge carriers ena ble magnetic coupling among magnetic impurities
through the Ruderman-Kittel-Kasuya-Yosida (RKKY) interaction [6–8]. Superconductors have a
quasiparticle gap and therefore the RKCKY mechanism between impurities is exponentially suppressed.
However, in superconductors with RIashba SOC, non-exponential decaying interaction between
magnetic impurities has been predicted [9] from a RKKY-like calculation of the spin-spin correlation
function. A later work, wiAth a complete analysis of such magnetic coupling, which includes the London-
Pearl screening effects, showed that the interaction of the anomalous supercurrents stemming from
different impurities can mediate a long-range ferromagnetic coupling [10]. This prediction opens up the
possibility of electric controlling of the magnetic state of a system of magnetic impurities in a
superconductor, a situation we explore in the present work.

The detection of current-induced magnetization in magnetic heterostructures typically relies on Hall
resistance, which is regarded as proportional to the magnetization. Such a Hall response does not occur
in a superconductor due to the vanishing resistance [11]. Therefore, a technique directly sensitive to the
magnetic induction from the magnetization and anomalous supercurrents is essential for detecting long-
range magnetization in Rashba superconductors. In this manuscript, we use scanning superconducting
quantum interference device (sSQUID) microscopy [12–21] to image the long-range magnetization of
Rashba superconductor Fe(Se,Te) in the high interstitial Fe density regime.

SOC allows the interesting possibility that a ferromagnetic order in a system of magnetic impurities can
be established via coupling to the superconducting condensate. Indeed, the ferromagnetic order is the
one that minimized the energy of the anomalous currents induced by the magnetoelectric effect due to
the SOC around each impurity.

Just like in a ferromagnet, where an external magnetic field is necessary to align magnetic domains, a
uniform magnetization across the sample is facilitated by applying a global supercurrent. In magnetic
heterostructures with Rashba SOC, the magnetization follows hysteretic switching under external
current [29,30]. The magnetic effect of an external supercurrent on a Rashba or Dirac superconductor
with magnetic impurities has yet to be experimentally studied. In general, in the absence of a constant
bias current or external magnetic field, both magnetization and anomalous supercurrents produce
magnetic induction, the spatial distribution of which depends on sample geometry. Measuring such a
magnetic signal and its evolution after applying a current may provide key evidence for the
supercurrent-mediated long-range ferromagnetic coupling of magnetic impurities.

Fe-chalcogenide superconductor Fe(Se,Te) has exhibited strong spin-orbit coupling, which leads to
superconducting topological surface states [31–35]. The excess Fe atoms occupy interstitial sites and act
as magnetic impurities [36]. Their interaction with the superconducting condensate enables phenomena
such as the quantum anomalous vortex state [25]. Scanning tunneling microscopy studies have found
zero-energy bound states in vortex cores or interstitial Fe sites on its surface [33,37–39]. Signs of time-
reversal symmetry breaking have also been reported on the surface states from photoemission
spectroscopy [40] and nitrogen-vacancy center magnetometry [41]. However, the impurity moments
naturally break time-reversal symmetry locally and the establishment of a long-range ferromagnetic
order requires a suitable impurity density and effective means to align possible magnetic domains.

The impurity moments are not coupled if the density is too low but a very high interstitial Fe
concentration will completely suppress superconductivity [21,42,43]. The impurity concentration we
consider here have an average interstitial Fe distance close to the coherence length so that their critical
temperatures are lower than the samples studied earlier [P44,45]. The interstitial Fe in Fe(Se,Te) is known
to lead to chemical inhomogeneity [46]. We first exfoli ate single crystals into a thin flake sample #1
with lateral dimensions in the range of tens of microns. We apply an alternating magnetic field using the
field coil on the nano-SQUID chip and demodu late the magnetic flux changes on the sample to obtain
the local magnetic susceptibility (Fig. 2a). The negative susceptibility within the sample boundary is the
Meissner response to the local modulaCtion directly related to the superfluid density. We find that the
superfluid density is relatively unifoIrm although it varies from flake-to-flake. This suggests that the
superconductivity is not surface-only. The suppression of superconductivity by magnetic impurities is
visible from the much-redAuced diamagnetic susceptibility compared with that of the samples with <1%
of interstitial Fe (Inset of Fig. 2a) [25].

Samples with such high concentration of interstitial Fe do not exhibit any quantum anomalous
vortices [25]. However, we observe magnetic domains in the magnetometry image at the base
temperature 𝑇 = 1.68 K after zero-field cooling (Fig. 2b). The flux signal is demodulated at the
vibration frequency of the tuning fork carrying the nano-SQUID, providing a measure of the flux
gradient along the vibration (z) axis. This demodulated signal is approximatively proportional to the
direct-current flux signal and exhibits a significantly reduced noise level, allowing the weak magnetic
domain contrast to be resolved. We delineate the sample contours based on the susceptometry images.
Features outside the boundary might come from magnetic moments and supercurrent near the edge
which has non-vanishing out-of-plane magnetic field outside the boundary of the sample. The domains
are random after each cooling cycle at the identical zero-field condition (Supplementary Fig. 1), which
rules out Meissner response from extrinsic magnetic contamination or surface roughness. The initial
domain size might be determined by the London penetration depth, coherence length, average distance
between interstitial iron atoms and fluctuations during the cooling process. Actually, it may be smaller
than the spatial resolution of our probe. Supplementary Fig. 2 shows the magnetic landscape of sample
#1 after field cooling under different applied field. Distinct from the Fe(Se,Te) sample in the low
interstitial Fe density regime [25], here it always shows magnetic domains rather than vortices, even if
the applied field is large enough to induce vortices. This suggests that the presence of in-plane
magnetization in our samples may compete with vortex formation. Previous works [25] showed that the
magnetic impurity moment in Fe(Se,Te) tend to align with the magnetic field of the vortices (Fig. 1a).
Therefore, a long-range in-plane magnetization of impurity moments disfavors vortices (which are
phase windings) nucleating in the sample (Fig. 1d). This argument is also corroborated by recent
calculations [10]. The superfluid density reduces as we increase the temperature on the sample (Figs.
2c-e), which is expected. The flux contrast from the magnetic domains weakens even faster (Figs. 2f-h).
At 𝑇 = 3.15 K when there is still visible diamagnetic susceptibility (Fig. 2e), the magnetic contrast has
disappeared (Fig. 2h) and it stays that way at even higher temperatures. The magnetic contrast depends
on superfluid density in two respects. First, the superfluid is the mediator for the ferromagnetic coupling
between magnetic impurities. Second, the magnetization generates anomalous supercurrent due to the
magneto-electric effect. And the magnetic contrast we obPserved is from the anomalous supercurrent.
The reduction of superfluid density thus has a compou nd effect on the magnetic contrast we detect,
making it decreasing faster as 𝑇 is approached. The absence of magnetic contrast above 𝑇 also rules
out the contribution of magnetic impurities. Th ese observations collectively suggest that the
spontaneous formation of magnetic domains requires superfluid density.

Single crystals of FeTe Se were grown using the Bridgman method. A mixture of Fe (99.99%), Te

Scanning SQUID microscopy
Scanning SQUID (sSQUID) measurements were performed in a closed-cycle He-4 refrigerator. The
thermometer was placed on the sample holder. The heater for the variable-temperature measurements
shown in Fig. 2 was placed on the substrate, while the heater for those in Fig. 4 was on the sample
holder. A small temperature gradient between the sample and the thermometer is expected for the
former.

The nano-SQUID sensors used for this study were scanning 2-junction SQUID susceptometers with two
balanced pickup loops of 2 μm diameter in a gradiometric configuration, each surrounded by a one-turn

restrictions to spatial resolution. The distance is usually about several micrometers determined by the
polishing of chip edge and the mounting angle of the probe, making the overall effective resolution a bit
larger than 2 μm. It is also worth noting that our measurements are capturing the field distribution
several micrometers above the edge current plane, in which Bz field contrast near the edge appears less

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Xiang et al. report on a scanning SQUID study of flakes of Fe(Se,Te) with relatively high Fe density. The main observation is
flux patterns that change in a hysteretic way after applying a current bias through the flakes. A comprehensive study of this
behavior is presented, including an analysis of magnetic field training through Meissner currents. Data from three flakes are
shown. The remnant flux is attributed to magnetization induced by a RKKY-like interaction, enabled in the superconducting
state by strong SOC. This would be an interesting demonstration of the interplay between magnetic impurities and
superconductivity. However, there are several major issues with the interpretation of the data, which I describe below. These
problems preclude me from recommending publication at this point.
Most importantly, the authors do not properly account for the inhomogeneity of the samples, which I believe is sufficient to
explain the observations. The susceptibility of all the flakes in this study is highly inhomogeneous. For example the top part
of the flake in Fig. 3 does not appear to be superconducting even at the base temperature. This means the critical current is
different for different regions in the sample. The change to the current distribution, and the remnant magnetization, are
correlated with the top part of that flake turning normal. This motivates the following interpretation: once the critical current for
the top part is reached, the current flows through the edges of the bottom part, generating a magnetic field through the flake.
When the current is gradually removed, the top part turns superconducting in the presence of this field. This results in
Meissner currents and/or vortices, and because the Pearl length is so large, they manifest as a “homogeneous” flux signal.
The other data shown are consistent with this alternative interpretation, for example the remnant flux pattern in extended
data 11 is correlated with the superfluid density landscape, rather than with current density pattern that would be generated
in this geometry.
To exclude this explanation, I suggest the authors either repeat the experiment on a single crystal sample, or on more
homogeneous flakes, and provide a better characterization of the local critical temperature and current density distributions
in the existing data.
Additional issues are listed below:
1) An image of the vortex distribution after cooling down in the presence of a magnetic field is missing. This would be helpful
in order to compare with the magnetic landscape reported, and rule out vortices.
2) What is the spatial resolution in these measurements? The authors say the pick-up loop diameter was 2 um, but they can’t
resolve the electrodes in extended data figure d,e.
3) The range shown in most images is insufficient to understand the current flow or magnetization. Magnetic field lines that
go out of plane and generate a positive signal should eventually close, generating a negative signal somewhere else. The
authors should measure further away from the flakes to capture the complete signal.
4) Similarly, the authors argue that the remnant flux signal is due to edge currents, but the data do not resemble the field
generated according to Biot-Savart law. Can the authors explain this?
5) The dashed lines in Figure 3 (and the corresponding extended data figures) are highly misleading. The optical image
clearly shows the flake extends to the right of where the dashed line is marked, and the susceptibility image in Fig. 3b shows
that portions of this area are superconducting. Yet the remnant flux appears only within the dashed lines. The authors should
explain this and provide imaging of the full device.
6) The streamlines overlaid on Fig. 3f,h,k are confusing. Firstly, they create a false impression that the current flows
homogeneously along the streamlines. The authors should try a different way to visualize this, perhaps by making the
thickness of the lines proportional to the magnitude of the current density. Secondly, in panels h and k, there are additional
streamlines overlaid. It is not clarified in the text how these lines were generated, and I do not see a way to divide the current
pattern into two origins just from the experimental data.
7) In extended data fig. 6, the current appears to flow at the edge of the sample, even though Ic was exceeded. Can the
authors explain that? The authors should compare this with images of the current flow taken above the transition
temperature, to ensure the sample is completely normal.

Response to Reviewer #1
The manuscript reports on experimental detection of ferromagnetic coupling between
localized magnetic moments in a superconductor with Rashba SOC. It uses scanning
SQUID microscopy to detect anomalous supercurrents due to this ferromagnetic coupling
above a bias threshold which interestingly remains even when the bias is removed. The
evidence of switching the magnetic moments by applying a bias supercurrent above a
threshold opens novel avenues for the design of cryogenic magnetic memories.
This is an interesting study which uncovers this rather unusual mechanism of
ferromagnetic coupling mediated by superconductivity.
-We thank the Reviewer #1 for concisely summarizing our work and highlighting its
importance. We are also grateful for the valuable comments that help us to improve it.
We have addressed the specific questions and comments below.
Before this manuscript can be considered for acceptance, the authors to clarify the points
below:
1. From the magnetic domain imaging in Figure 2 and the corresponding extended figure,
it seems that these magnetic domains are several microns long and wide. It is not clear
what sets this initial domain size.
-We thank the reviewer for bringing up this issue. The initial domain size might be
determined by the London penetration depth, coherence length, average distance
between interstitial iron atoms and fluctuations during the cooling process. Actually, it
may be smaller than the spatial resolution of our probe. We have added this discussion
to Lines 166-169 in the revised manuscript.
2. The explanation of aligning the spins along the centre line is also not clear. It multiple
spins are present within the coherence length, it seems that an antiferromagnetic coupling
will reduce the overall free energy. Why is then a ferromagnetic alignment preferred in
equilibrium (no external supercurrent)?
-Even without an external supercurrent, there is spontaneous anomalous supercurrent
excited around interstitial iron atoms. Taking London-Pearl screening effects into
consideration, the interaction between them may lead to ferromagnetic coupling under
certain conditions [Phys. Rev. B 108, L180506 (2023)]. Indeed, the ferromagnetic order
is the one that minimized the energy of the anomalous currents induced by the
magnetoelectric effect, due to the SOC, around each impurity. Consequently, the ground
state is a domain state and the uniform ferromagnetic alignment can be facilitated by
external bias current. We have added this clarification to Lines 100-104.
3. Page 4, line 144: Figure 2a is showing result from one flake and flake-to-flake variation
is not clear from here. Image from a second flake in the main figure or in the extended
information is needed to show the variation. Also, the authors should explain in a few
sentences what the figure shows and how the signal relates to the superfluid density.
-We thank the reviewer for this nice suggestion. In the revised manuscript, we have
assigned a specific number for each flake (#1-#3) to show the variation. Also, we have
added some explanations for Figure 2a to Lines 147-151:‘We apply an alternating
magnetic field using the field coil on SQUID chip and demodulate the magnetic flux
changes on the sample to obtain the local magnetic susceptibility (Figure 2a). The
negative susceptibility is contributed by Meissner supercurrent directly related to the
superfluid density.’
4. Figure 2: it is not clear that why the susceptometry and magnetometry images do not
exactly align with respect to the dotted line marking the flake boundary. It seems that the
magnetometry image is outside the boundary on the right hand side and the susceptometry
data does not go all the way to the boundary. The authors should explain this.
-We thank the reviewer for pointing out this issue. In practice, we delineate the sample
contours based on the local susceptibility image. Due to the finite spatial resolution, the
boundary transitions are characterized by a gradual decay rather than abrupt changes,
introducing some uncertainty to the contours. We have made slight adjustments to the
selection of the contour in Figure 2 to make it visually more consistent with the
magnetic susceptibility image presented under the current colormap. As for the
magnetic contrast outside the boundary, it might come from magnetic moments and
supercurrent near the edge which has a finite out-of-plane magnetic field outside the
boundary of the sample. We have added these explanations to Line 161-164.
5. Page 4, line 147 - the comparison image should be provided as an inset from reference
14.
-We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We have provided a comparison image from
reference 14 ([Phys. Rev. X 13, 011046 (2023)]) as an inset to Figure 2a.
6. Page 5, first line (156) and figure 2: the magnetic contrast appear to decay faster than
the superfluid density as Tc is approached. What is the reason for this faster disappearence
of the magnetic signal?
-The magnetic contrast depends on superfluid density in two respects. First, the
superfluid is the mediator for the ferromagnetic coupling between magnetic impurities.
Second, the magnetization generates anomalous supercurrent due to the magneto-
electric effect. And the magnetic contrast we observed is from the anomalous
supercurrent. The reduction of superfluid density thus has a compound effect on the
magnetic contrast we detect, making it decreasing faster as Tc is approached. We have
added this discussion to Line 177-183.
7. Last line of Fig. 2 caption should read, “…the magnetic domains results from…”
-We thank the reviewer for pointing out this language problem. We have modified this
sentence in Figure 2 caption as suggested.
Response to Reviewer #2
Xiang et al. report on a scanning SQUID study of flakes of Fe(Se,Te) with relatively high
Fe density. The main observation is flux patterns that change in a hysteretic way after
applying a current bias through the flakes. A comprehensive study of this behavior is
presented, including an analysis of magnetic field training through Meissner currents. Data
from three flakes are shown. The remnant flux is attributed to magnetization induced by a
RKKY-like interaction, enabled in the superconducting state by strong SOC. This would be
an interesting demonstration of the interplay between magnetic impurities and
superconductivity.
-We thank the reviewer for the careful reading and high evaluation of our manuscript.
We also appreciate the constructive suggestions and the opportunity to improve it.
However, there are several major issues with the interpretation of the data, which I describe
below. These problems preclude me from recommending publication at this point.
Most importantly, the authors do not properly account for the inhomogeneity of the samples,
which I believe is sufficient to explain the observations. The susceptibility of all the flakes
in this study is highly inhomogeneous. For example the top part of the flake in Fig. 3 does
not appear to be superconducting even at the base temperature. This means the critical
current is different for different regions in the sample. The change to the current distribution,
and the remnant magnetization, are correlated with the top part of that flake turning normal.
This motivates the following interpretation: once the critical current for the top part is
reached, the current flows through the edges of the bottom part, generating a magnetic
field through the flake. When the current is gradually removed, the top part turns
superconducting in the presence of this field. This results in Meissner currents and/or
vortices, and because the Pearl length is so large, they manifest as a “homogeneous”
flux signal.
The other data shown are consistent with this alternative interpretation, for example the
remnant flux pattern in extended data 11 is correlated with the superfluid density landscape,
rather than with current density pattern that would be generated in this geometry.
To exclude this explanation, I suggest the authors either repeat the experiment on a single
crystal sample, or on more homogeneous flakes, and provide a better characterization of
the local critical temperature and current density distributions in the existing data.
- We thank the reviewer for bringing up an alternative interpretation of our findings. We
acknowledge the inhomogeneity of the samples, which arises from the stochastic
distribution of interstitial iron atoms. However, our data is not consistent with the
vortex
trapping scenario, as we elucidate below.
1. In Extended Data Figures 8b and e, we use two electrodes on the bottom edge of the
sample so that the bias current favors to flow along the bottom edge. This current
configuration generates a positive magnetic field within the sample. However, we
observed remanent flux signal with a negative polarity (Extended Data Figures 8b),
which contradicts the vortex trapping scenario. The same argument also applies to the
remnant flux pattern depicted in Extended Data Figure 8c, which is more consistent
with the anomalous supercurrent picture we propose [Phys. Rev. B 102, 060506, (2020);
Phys. Rev. B 108, L180506 (2023)].
2. We have expanded the image range of sample #2 in Extended Data Figures 4 and 7.
We can see that the superfluid density on the left part of the flake is depleted at I = 200
b
μA. Hence, this region would be expected to be more susceptible to vortex trapping.
However, this region shows negligibly small remnant flux.
3. Our observation of the sudden onset of edge current above some threshold does not
agree with vortex trapping. From Extended Data Figures 4d, we can see that the
diamagnetism of the sample at I = 200 μA is still present on the bottom edge, which is
b
the region where the edge current shows a strong contrast (Fig. 3).
4. The temperature dependence of the remnant flux (Fig. 4f) provides additional
evidence against vortex penetration. The variation of integrated magnetic flux with
increasing temperature is much smaller than the flux quantum, which is inconsistent
with leakage of vortices with increasing temperature.
5. We have repeated the experiment on a more homogeneous flake sample (Extended
Data Figure 12). We have observed the spontaneous magnetic domains (Extended Data
Figure 12b) as well as the alignment of domains by a bias current (Extended Data
Figures 12c and d). In this sample, the switching current is about 1.6 mA (Extended
Data Figure 12f) which is far below the critical current of 6 mA (Extended Data Figure
12e), making the possibility of vortex trapping highly unlikely. Furthermore, the sign
of the remanent flux is consistent with that on samples #1 and #2 and opposite from the
Biot-Savart field of the current.
We have added these discussions to Lines 216-221 and Lines 304-311 in the revised
manuscript.
Additional issues are listed below:
1) An image of the vortex distribution after cooling down in the presence of a magnetic field
is missing. This would be helpful in order to compare with the magnetic landscape reported,
and rule out vortices.
-We are grateful for the reviewer's constructive suggestion. In the revised manuscript,
we have accordingly incorporated the magnetic landscape of flake #1 after field cooling
to Extended Data Figure 2. Different from the Fe(Se,Te) flake in the low interstitial Fe
density regime [Phys. Rev. X 13, 011046 (2023)], it always shows magnetic domains
rather than vortices, even if the applied field is strong enough to induce vortex
penetration. It suggests that in the high interstitial Fe density regime, ferromagnetic
structure is a more favorable state for magnetic impurities due to the Rashba coupling.
We have added these discussions to Lines 169-173.
2) What is the spatial resolution in these measurements? The authors say the pick-up loop diameter was 2 um, but they can’t
resolve the electrodes in extended data figure d,e.
-The pick-up loop diameter is 2 μm which limits the optimal spatial resolution. Besides,
the distance between the pick-up loop and sample is also a restriction. The distance is
usually about several micrometers determined by the polishing of chip edge and the
mounting angle of the probe, making the overall resolution a bit worse than 2 μm.
We can resolve the electrodes through the boundaries of positive and negative current
flux signals in Extended Data Figure 8f, attesting to the resolution. However, such a
feature is inherently absent when the bias is on the same side of the sample (Extended
Data Figures 8d-e) because the current flux has the same sign in the regions between
the two electrodes. We have made modifications to Lines 457-461 in the revised
manuscript.
3) The range shown in most images is insufficient to understand the current flow or
magnetization. Magnetic field lines that go out of plane and generate a positive signal
should eventually close, generating a negative signal somewhere else. The authors should
measure further away from the flakes to capture the complete signal.
-We appreciate the reviewer’s helpful advices. We have updated Extended Data Figure
7 to provide a comprehensive visualization of the complete current flow. Extended Data
Figure 4 has also been modified to show susceptibility and remnant flux across the
entire device.
The reviewer is totally correct about the flux line having to close. However, there is
limitless space outside the sample and therefore the return flux typically extends over a
much larger area than the sample. This is the reason that the return flux signal outside
the sample boundary is significantly weaker than the flux signal within the boundary.
In order to enhance the signal contrast, we utilize AC measurements that are
demodulated at the vibration frequency of the tuning fork carrying the nano-SQUID.
Since such a demodulated flux signal is more sensitive to the gradient of the magnetic
field, this method allows for a clearer visualization of the flux signal of opposite sign
across the sample boundary (Extended Data Figures 12c and d).
4) Similarly, the authors argue that the remnant flux signal is due to edge currents, but the
data do not resemble the field generated according to Biot-Savart law. Can the authors
explain this?
- Due to the geometry constraint of the planer nano-SQUID, we are capturing the field
distribution several micrometers above the edge current plane, in which Bz field
contrast near the edge appears less distinct. We have added these supplementary notes
to Lines 461-464.
When measuring with the AC flux mode discussed above, we can see clear edge flux
reversal in consistent with edge current according to Biot-Savart law (Extended Data
Figures 12c and d).
5) The dashed lines in Figure 3 (and the corresponding extended data figures) are highly
misleading. The optical image clearly shows the flake extends to the right of where the
dashed line is marked, and the susceptibility image in Fig. 3b shows that portions of this
area are superconducting. Yet the remnant flux appears only within the dashed lines. The
authors should explain this and provide imaging of the full device.
-We thank the reviewer for bringing up this issue. We have modified Extended Data
Figure 4 and Extended Data Figure 7 to show the magnetometry and susceptometry
images of the full device.
The dashed lines are introduced according to the susceptometry image (Extended Data
Fig. 4d). As explained in more detail in the revised manuscript Lines 192-194, the
segregation of diamagnetic patches is related to inhomogeneous interstitial Fe density.
We find the remnant flux is predominantly located within the dashed circle probably
due to its higher superfluid density, which correlates with the remnant flux intensity.
6) The streamlines overlaid on Fig. 3f,h,k are confusing. Firstly, they create a false
impression that the current flows homogeneously along the streamlines. The authors
should try a different way to visualize this, perhaps by making the thickness of the lines
proportional to the magnitude of the current density. Secondly, in panels h and k, there are
additional streamlines overlaid. It is not clarified in the text how these lines were generated,
and I do not see a way to divide the current pattern into two origins just from the
experimental data.
-We thank the reviewer for the very constructive suggestions. We have revised the
current streamlines in Figs. 3f,h,k and made the thickness of the lines proportional to
the magnitude of the current density. Additional streamlines in panels h and k are
anomalous supercurrent 𝑱 with opposite directions in the bulk (dark green lines) and
a
along the edges (light green lines). Our interpretation is based on the previous
theoretical works [Phys. Rev. B 102, 060506, (2020); Phys. Rev. B 108, L180506
(2023)]. This model is supported by the emergence of the edge current and the remnant
flux pattern under different current configurations. We have emphasized these
explanations on Lines 293-297.
7) In extended data fig. 6, the current appears to flow at the edge of the sample, even
though Ic was exceeded. Can the authors explain that? The authors should compare this
with images of the current flow taken above the transition temperature, to ensure the
sample is completely normal.
-We thank the reviewer for the instructive comments. We have made clearer definition
of critical current in the revised manuscript. At I = 260 μA, the sample is in the mixed
b
state: it exhibits reduced superfluid density, but it has not reached a complete normal
state despite the presence of a voltage across it. The current still flows at the bottom
edge due to the stronger superfluid density there (Extended Data Fig. 7c). As a
comparison, current does flow uniformly across the sample when it is completely
normal above the transition temperature [Science Bulletin 66, 425-432 (2021)]. These
results suggest that the edge remnant flux and anomalous current do not arise from the
loss of superconductivity. We have added these explanatory sentences to Lines 227-232
in the revised manuscript.
Major changes in the revised manuscript:
1. Images of direct-current measurement of flux for sample #3 are added to
Extended Data Figure 12. Explanation of two measurement modes is added to
Lines 483-489.
2. Analysis of the remanent magnetic flux signal amplitude versus

The authors provide additional data and discussion, which alleviate some of my concerns.
The only truly convincing support for the scenario that they propose is the new extended
data fig. 12, which is from a new flake that is more homogeneous, and where the switching
current is far below the critical current.
-We are grateful to the reviewer for approving the improvement of the revised
manuscript with the additional experimental data and discussions. As highlighted in
Extended Data Figure 12, the new flake with improved homogeneity exhibits that the
switching current is substantially lower than the critical current, thereby ruling out
alternative explanations such as the vortex-trapping scenario.
There are two points that must be addressed about these new data:
(1) To complete the picture, the authors should also include images of the current density
in the superconducting and normal state. Particularly, with a bias of 2mA it is critical to
show that the current flows entirely on the edge (as expected if the sample is indeed SC)
and not through some complicated path in the sample.
-We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We would like to clarify that
the current does not flow entirely along the edge when a bias current is applied. Instead,
current distribution involves a combination of anomalous edge and bulk supercurrents
(Figs. 2g and j), which are induced by the long-range in-plane magnetization intrinsic
to the Rashba superconductor. It is only after the bias current is removed can we observe
the anomalous supercurrent which flows only along the edge. For Sample #3,
regretfully we were unable to perform imaging at the high bias current of 2 mA due to
some technical difficulties (the heating under such high current from resistive part of
the current leads induces large noise in the nano-SQUID). However, the flux images
under an applied current are presented for sample #2 in Figure 3 and 4 of the manuscript,
which is consistent with the analysis above.
The reviewer's concern appears to center on the vortex penetration effects. We
emphasize that superconductors with comparable Pearl lengths (~100 μm) exhibit well-
established vortex signatures as demonstrated in previous studies [Appl. Phys. Lett. 5,
65-66, (1964); Phys. Rev. Lett. 92, 157006, (2004); Nat. Commun. 16, 2696, (2025)].
Specifically, vortex-induced magnetic profiles manifest characteristic 1/r (r being the
distance from vortex core) spatial dependence within the Pearl length regime.
Importantly, homogenous remanent flux distribution here is inconsistent with vortex-
induced magnetic profile and strongly supports our interpretation of circulating current.
We have substantially expanded our discussion of these points into the revised
manuscript in Lines 313-320 and Lines 236-245.
(2) The critical current of this new sample (6mA) is ~30 times larger than the other devices
(~200 uA). The susceptibility signal also seems to be ~10 times larger and yet the magnetic
signals are 10 times smaller. It appears to contradict the scenario put forth by the authors:
if the superfluid density mediates the ferromagnetic interaction, I would expect stronger
superconductivity to also give rise to stronger magnetism.
-We thank the reviewer for catching this detail. The magnetic images shown for the two
samples are from different measurement modes and therefore cannot be compared
directly. The flux images in Extended Data Figure 12 employ lock-in detection at the
tuning fork frequency (AC demodulation) to enhance sensitivity, whereas Fig. 3
presents DC flux measurements of sample #2.
In order to quantitative compare the remanent flux of the two samples, we have included
DC flux data for sample #3 in the revised Extended Data Figure 12. The DC flux
magnitude of sample #3 is indeed about 10 times larger than sample #2, in consistent
with their relative diamagnetic susceptibility. This further supports our scenario that
superfluid density mediates the ferromagnetic interaction. We have explicitly addressed
this quantitative detail in Lines 483-489 and added analysis in Lines 225-229.
The authors claim that vortices never enter the samples, even when cooled with a
sufficiently large external field. This should be explained further.
-We thank the reviewer for bringing up this point. We argue that the presence of in-
plane magnetization in our samples may compete with vortex formation. Previous
works [14] showed that the magnetic impurity moment in Fe(Se,Te) tend to align with
the magnetic field of the vortices (Fig. 1a). Therefore, a long-range in-plane
magnetization of impurity moments disfavors vortices (which are phase windings)
nucleating in the sample (Fig. 1d). This argument is also corroborated by recent
calculations taking into account the London-Pearl screening effects [10]. We have
added these explanations to the revised manuscript in Lines 171-176.
In addition, the authors should provide the (London) penetration depth of these samples,
preferably extracted from the susceptibility measurements, and compare this with the size
of domains, size of the flakes and the spatial resolution. I am not convinced that the vortices
are not simply too large to be resolved here.
-We thank the reviewer for the insightful suggestion. We would like to clarify the
concept of penetration depth involved in our manuscript. The London penetration depth
(𝜆) describes the exponential decay of the magnetic field near the surface of a strong
bulk superconductor, characterizing the Meissner screening effect. While in two-
dimensional superconductors or superconductors with low superfluid density defined
by 𝜆 ≫ 𝑑 , where 𝑑 is the thickness of the sample, Pearl length (Λ ) governs the
P
lateral spread of magnetic flux from vortices. The relationship between these two
magnetic length scales is given by Λ = 2𝜆2/𝑑 [Appl. Phys. Lett. 5, 65-66, (1964)].
P
For sample #1, susceptibility measurement (Extended Data Figure 1) yields Λ ≈
P
87 μm . Sample #3 exhibits similar susceptibility and Λ , while sample #2 shows
P
weaker susceptibility, implying a larger Λ . London penetration depth 𝜆 of these
P
samples derived from the aforementioned relationship is several micrometers. The size
of the observed magnetic domains (Extended Data Figure 1 and Extended Data Figure
12) is also on the order of several micrometers, which is close to the spatial resolution
of our probe.
For all three samples, the Pearl length Λ exceeds the physical dimensions of the
P
flakes. If vortices were present, the flux profile would decay as 1/Λ 𝑟 near the vortex
P
core and as Λ /𝑟3 for distance greater than Λ , where 𝑟 is the distance from the
P P
vortex center [Appl. Phys. Lett. 5, 65-66, (1964); Phys. Rev. Lett. 92, 157006, (2004);
Nat. Commun. 16, 2696, (2025)]. However, the remanent flux pattern does not follow
such a decay law, indicating inconsistency with the explanation of vortex-penetration.
We have incorporated these analyses into the revised manuscript in Lines 236-245.
To conclude, additional data and analysis are still required to fully support the interpretation
suggested by the authors.
-We sincerely thank the reviewer for the constructive suggestions that help us further
improve our manuscript. In the revised version, we have incorporated additional data
and analysis to further exclude vortex-related effect and support the scenario of
superfluid density mediated ferromagnetic coupling. We appreciate the reviewer's time
and feedback, and we trust the revised manuscript now meets the required standards.

and vortex penetration lead to the observed signals. Therefore, I find myself unable to recommend the publication without at
least a serious discussion and consideration of all other alternative interpretations.
The penetration of vortices in these samples is complicated. The inhomogeneity of the samples, combined with the “training”
schemes that are used, where the current and magnetic field distributions in the sample are inhomogeneous, allow a non-
uniform density of vortices to penetrate the sample. The density of these vortices may be too high to resolve individually with
the 2 um resolution of the SQUID sensor. Therefore the discussion of the Pearl length and signature of an individual vortex

can already produce an inhomogeneous magnetic field and switch magnetization. This has
been used in many effects in many other studies.

Fe(Se,Te) systems with compositions similar to ours has been previously established
by ARPES measurements and band-structure calculations (e.g., Refs. 31, 40), and the
general principles of magnetic coupling with SOC in such systems have been
analyzed in Refs. 10-13.

magnetization manifested through the supercurrent (which is intrinsically linked to the
superfluid density). This specific manifestation is distinct from phenomena reported

flow. With proper patterning, the authors might be able to make a case and systematically

or sample roughness. As a natural progression for this research line, we note in the

devices represents an important next step for future investigation.

current-intensity-dependent magnetic-field distribution. The phenomenon itself is real.

simply claimed that they are mapping the supercurrent or its interaction with magnetic
features, that would likely be correct. But the authors did not interpret it convincingly.

an overclaim.

Instead, it is substantiated by the unique interplay between the magnetic moments and
the superconducting condensate, and most critically by their response to experimental
manipulation. Specifically, we have demonstrated the existence of zero-field-cooled
magnetic domains mediated by the superconducting condensate and the random
redistribution of these domains over repeated thermal cycles (Fig. 2 and Extended

switching of magnetic domains, the presence of remanent magnetization, and a clear
hysteresis loop (Figs. 3 and 4, Extended Data Figs. 12 and 13) are established

the authors have failed to rule out the trivial scenario in which inhomogeneity and vortex
penetration lead to the observed signal. In their reply to the other reviewer, the authors
claimed that remnant magnetization is strong evidence against the trivial scenario of vortex
trapping, but I believe the authors are incorrect. As the other reviewer pointed out, the
actual situation is far more complicated.

experiments using a homogeneous sample. The results demonstrate that under the
applied current bias, there is no local suppression of superconductivity. Furthermore,
we observe a clear remnant magnetization signal after the current is removed
(Extended Data Fig. 13). This clearly argues against the vortex trapping scenario.

In some of the results in this study, the observations contradict fundamental properties of
magnetism and magnetic fields. In-plane magnetization should produce a dipole-like
magnetic-field distribution. This contradicts what is shown in both the extended figures and
the main text. In the main-text figures, the features appear in-plane, whereas in the
extended figures the same features become out-of-plane. The authors claimed that they

hypothesis without experimental proof.

contrast after the bias current is removed originates from the anomalous edge
supercurrent of a Rashba superconductor, rather than the in-plane magnetization
directly. Similarly, the spontaneous magnetic domains we image are manifested
through the local anomalous supercurrents circulating at domain boundaries, which

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Conventional superconductors disfavor ferromagnetism because the supercurrent-carrying
electrons are paired into anti-parallel spin singlets. Consequently, ferromagnetic coupling
between localized moments through the charge carriers is absent in s-wave superconductors.
However, Rashba-type spin-orbit coupling (SOC) can profoundly alter the interaction between
the charge carriers and localized spins. Here, we report long-range ferromagnetic order among
the impurity moments on the surface of an s-wave SOC superconductor, Fe(Se,Te). We employ
scanning superconducting quantum interference device microscopy and find suppressed vortex
states but spontaneous magnetic domains in the superconducting state. Homogeneous remanent
flux patterns are induced by applying supercurrents through the sample. The patterns are
consistent with anomalous edge and bulk supercurrents generated by long-range in-plane
magnetization related to the magneto-electric effect intrinsic to a Rashba superconductor. The
anomalous supercurrents occur above a bias current threshold and follow hysteresis loops
reminiscent of those of a ferromagnet. Surprisingly, the magnetic switching (super)current
density is three orders of magnitude less than that in a ferromagnetic metal with SOC.
These observations suggest an emergent ferromagnetic impurity state in a Rashba superconductor,
which can be controlled by applying supercurrents.

---

## Introduction

One of the immediate challenges facing high-speed computation using superconductors is a lack of fast
cryogenic memory with low drive power [1]. Non-superconducting memories widely used nowadays
are too slow and power-demanding for single-flux quantum electronics [2]. Superconducting memories
based on Josephson junctions [3,4] provide a faster solution but suffer from vortex trapping and
scalability problem [5]. A magnetic superconductor which can be switched by a supercurrent may be a
candidate material to overcome these current limitations. However, extrinsic ferromagnetic moments
breaks Cooper pairs in s-wave superconductors and supercurrent exerts Lorentz force on free vortices,
causing energy dissipation.

Utilizing supercurrent to mediate ferromagnetism among local magnetic moments may overcome these
problems. In normal metals, charge carriers ena ble magnetic coupling among magnetic impurities
through the Ruderman-Kittel-Kasuya-Yosida (RKKY) interaction [6–8]. Superconductors have a
quasiparticle gap and therefore the RKCKY mechanism between impurities is exponentially suppressed.
However, in superconductors with RIashba SOC, non-exponential decaying interaction between
magnetic impurities has been predicted [9] from a RKKY-like calculation of the spin-spin correlation
function. A later work, wiAth a complete analysis of such magnetic coupling, which includes the London-
Pearl screening effects, showed that the interaction of the anomalous supercurrents stemming from
different impurities can mediate a long-range ferromagnetic coupling [10]. This prediction opens up the
possibility of electric controlling of the magnetic state of a system of magnetic impurities in a
superconductor, a situation we explore in the present work.

The detection of current-induced magnetization in magnetic heterostructures typically relies on Hall
resistance, which is regarded as proportional to the magnetization. Such a Hall response does not occur
in a superconductor due to the vanishing resistance [11]. Therefore, a technique directly sensitive to the
magnetic induction from the magnetization and anomalous supercurrents is essential for detecting long-
range magnetization in Rashba superconductors. In this manuscript, we use scanning superconducting
quantum interference device (sSQUID) microscopy [12–21] to image the long-range magnetization of
Rashba superconductor Fe(Se,Te) in the high interstitial Fe density regime.

---

## Results

Observation of spontaneous magnetic domains in superconducting Fe(Se,Te) with interstitial
magnetic impurity
To comprehend the emergence of such ferromagnetic ordering, we briefly revisit the key aspects of the
theory. In Rashba superconductors and in superconductors with surfaces supporting a Dirac band, the
symmetry allows for a term in the Ginzburg-Landau free energy of the form of Lifshitz invariant 𝐹 =
𝜅(𝐧×𝐁)∙ℏ∇𝜑 [22–24], where ∇𝜑 is a phase gradient in the order parameter, 𝐁 is the magnetic
induction, 𝐧 is the surface normal, and 𝜅 is the Edelstein constant, which depends on the Rashba
splitting of the Kramer’s pair at the Fermi level. For Dirac surface states, it is a limiting case of a large
Rashba SOC when the physics is dominated by only one helical band. A direct consequence of the
Lifshitz invariant is that any supercurrent 𝐉 (being proportional to ∇𝜑) induces polarization of surface
impurity moments, which has been observed on isolated quantum anoSmalous vortex and antivortex in
Fe(Se,Te) (Fig. 1a) [25].

The inverse effect, in analogy with the spin-galvanic effect in SOC metals, is that a local magnetic
moment polarizes the condensate and generates anoma lous supercurrents 𝐉

Confined to the surface plane, two impurity spins favor an alignment along their center line (Fig. 1c).
Such a configuration minimizes the total supercurrent on both impurities and thus reduces the free
energy. For disordered impurity Tspins on a plane, ferromagnetic coupling leads to long-range in-plane

(Fig. 1d) [23]. With the exception of square lattices where anti-ferromagnetism is favored [10], Rashba
SOC allows the interesting possibility that a ferromagnetic order in a system of magnetic impurities can
be established via coupling to the superconducting condensate. Indeed, the ferromagnetic order is the
one that minimized the energy of the anomalous currents induced by the magnetoelectric effect due to
the SOC around each impurity.

Just like in a ferromagnet, where an external magnetic field is necessary to align magnetic domains, a
uniform magnetization across the sample is facilitated by applying a global supercurrent. In magnetic
heterostructures with Rashba SOC, the magnetization follows hysteretic switching under external
current [29,30]. The magnetic effect of an external supercurrent on a Rashba or Dirac superconductor
with magnetic impurities has yet to be experimentally studied. In general, in the absence of a constant
bias current or external magnetic field, both magnetization and anomalous supercurrents produce
magnetic induction, the spatial distribution of which depends on sample geometry. Measuring such a
magnetic signal and its evolution after applying a current may provide key evidence for the
supercurrent-mediated long-range ferromagnetic coupling of magnetic impurities.

Fe-chalcogenide superconductor Fe(Se,Te) has exhibited strong spin-orbit coupling, which leads to
superconducting topological surface states [31–35]. The excess Fe atoms occupy interstitial sites and act
as magnetic impurities [36]. Their interaction with the superconducting condensate enables phenomena
such as the quantum anomalous vortex state [25]. Scanning tunneling microscopy studies have found
zero-energy bound states in vortex cores or interstitial Fe sites on its surface [33,37–39]. Signs of time-
reversal symmetry breaking have also been reported on the surface states from photoemission
spectroscopy [40] and nitrogen-vacancy center magnetometry [41]. However, the impurity moments
naturally break time-reversal symmetry locally and the establishment of a long-range ferromagnetic
order requires a suitable impurity density and effective means to align possible magnetic domains.

The impurity moments are not coupled if the density is too low but a very high interstitial Fe
concentration will completely suppress superconductivity [21,42,43]. The impurity concentration we
consider here have an average interstitial Fe distance close to the coherence length so that their critical
temperatures are lower than the samples studied earlier [P44,45]. The interstitial Fe in Fe(Se,Te) is known

with lateral dimensions in the range of tens of microns. We apply an alternating magnetic field using the
field coil on the nano-SQUID chip and demodu late the magnetic flux changes on the sample to obtain

superfluid density is relatively unifoIrm although it varies from flake-to-flake. This suggests that the
superconductivity is not surface-only. The suppression of superconductivity by magnetic impurities is
visible from the much-redAuced diamagnetic susceptibility compared with that of the samples with <1%
of interstitial Fe (Inset of Fig. 2a) [25].

Samples with such high concentration of interstitial Fe do not exhibit any quantum anomalous
vortices [25]. However, we observe magnetic domains in the magnetometry image at the base

vibration frequency of the tuning fork carrying the nano-SQUID, providing a measure of the flux
gradient along the vibration (z) axis. This demodulated signal is approximatively proportional to the
direct-current flux signal and exhibits a significantly reduced noise level, allowing the weak magnetic
domain contrast to be resolved. We delineate the sample contours based on the susceptometry images.

which has non-vanishing out-of-plane magnetic field outside the boundary of the sample. The domains
are random after each cooling cycle at the identical zero-field condition (Supplementary Fig. 1), which
rules out Meissner response from extrinsic magnetic contamination or surface roughness. The initial
domain size might be determined by the London penetration depth, coherence length, average distance
between interstitial iron atoms and fluctuations during the cooling process. Actually, it may be smaller
than the spatial resolution of our probe. Supplementary Fig. 2 shows the magnetic landscape of sample
#1 after field cooling under different applied field. Distinct from the Fe(Se,Te) sample in the low
interstitial Fe density regime [25], here it always shows magnetic domains rather than vortices, even if
the applied field is large enough to induce vortices. This suggests that the presence of in-plane
magnetization in our samples may compete with vortex formation. Previous works [25] showed that the
magnetic impurity moment in Fe(Se,Te) tend to align with the magnetic field of the vortices (Fig. 1a).
Therefore, a long-range in-plane magnetization of impurity moments disfavors vortices (which are
phase windings) nucleating in the sample (Fig. 1d). This argument is also corroborated by recent
calculations [10]. The superfluid density reduces as we increase the temperature on the sample (Figs.

on superfluid density in two respects. First, the superfluid is the mediator for the ferromagnetic coupling
between magnetic impurities. Second, the magnetization generates anomalous supercurrent due to the
magneto-electric effect. And the magnetic contrast we obPserved is from the anomalous supercurrent.
The reduction of superfluid density thus has a compou nd effect on the magnetic contrast we detect,

### Reviewer 2

Xiang et al. report on a scanning SQUID study of flakes of Fe(Se,Te) with relatively high Fe density. The main observation is
flux patterns that change in a hysteretic way after applying a current bias through the flakes. A comprehensive study of this
behavior is presented, including an analysis of magnetic field training through Meissner currents. Data from three flakes are
shown. The remnant flux is attributed to magnetization induced by a RKKY-like interaction, enabled in the superconducting
state by strong SOC. This would be an interesting demonstration of the interplay between magnetic impurities and
superconductivity. However, there are several major issues with the interpretation of the data, which I describe below. These
problems preclude me from recommending publication at this point.
Most importantly, the authors do not properly account for the inhomogeneity of the samples, which I believe is sufficient to
explain the observations. The susceptibility of all the flakes in this study is highly inhomogeneous. For example the top part
of the flake in Fig. 3 does not appear to be superconducting even at the base temperature. This means the critical current is
different for different regions in the sample. The change to the current distribution, and the remnant magnetization, are
correlated with the top part of that flake turning normal. This motivates the following interpretation: once the critical current for
the top part is reached, the current flows through the edges of the bottom part, generating a magnetic field through the flake.
When the current is gradually removed, the top part turns superconducting in the presence of this field. This results in
Meissner currents and/or vortices, and because the Pearl length is so large, they manifest as a “homogeneous” flux signal.
The other data shown are consistent with this alternative interpretation, for example the remnant flux pattern in extended
data 11 is correlated with the superfluid density landscape, rather than with current density pattern that would be generated
in this geometry.
To exclude this explanation, I suggest the authors either repeat the experiment on a single crystal sample, or on more
homogeneous flakes, and provide a better characterization of the local critical temperature and current density distributions
in the existing data.
Additional issues are listed below:
1) An image of the vortex distribution after cooling down in the presence of a magnetic field is missing. This would be helpful
in order to compare with the magnetic landscape reported, and rule out vortices.
2) What is the spatial resolution in these measurements? The authors say the pick-up loop diameter was 2 um, but they can’t
resolve the electrodes in extended data figure d,e.
3) The range shown in most images is insufficient to understand the current flow or magnetization. Magnetic field lines that
go out of plane and generate a positive signal should eventually close, generating a negative signal somewhere else. The
authors should measure further away from the flakes to capture the complete signal.
4) Similarly, the authors argue that the remnant flux signal is due to edge currents, but the data do not resemble the field
generated according to Biot-Savart law. Can the authors explain this?

clearly shows the flake extends to the right of where the dashed line is marked, and the susceptibility image in Fig. 3b shows
that portions of this area are superconducting. Yet the remnant flux appears only within the dashed lines. The authors should
explain this and provide imaging of the full device.
6) The streamlines overlaid on Fig. 3f,h,k are confusing. Firstly, they create a false impression that the current flows
homogeneously along the streamlines. The authors should try a different way to visualize this, perhaps by making the
thickness of the lines proportional to the magnitude of the current density. Secondly, in panels h and k, there are additional

7) In extended data fig. 6, the current appears to flow at the edge of the sample, even though Ic was exceeded. Can the
authors explain that? The authors should compare this with images of the current flow taken above the transition
temperature, to ensure the sample is completely normal.

## Abstract

Conventional superconductors disfavor ferromagnetism because the supercurrent-carrying
electrons are paired into anti-parallel spin singlets. Consequently, ferromagnetic coupling
between localized moments through the charge carriers is absent in s-wave superconductors.
However, Rashba-type spin-orbit coupling (SOC) can profoundly alter the interaction between
the charge carriers and localized spins. Here, we report long-range ferromagnetic order among
the impurity moments on the surface of an s-wave SOC superconductor, Fe(Se,Te). We employ
scanning superconducting quantum interference device microscopy and find suppressed vortex
states but spontaneous magnetic domains in the superconducting state. Homogeneous remanent
flux patterns are induced by applying supercurrents through the sample. The patterns are
consistent with anomalous edge and bulk supercurrents generated by long-range in-plane
magnetization related to the magneto-electric effect intrinsic to a Rashba superconductor. The
anomalous supercurrents occur above a bias current threshold and follow hysteresis loops
reminiscent of those of a ferromagnet. Surprisingly, the magnetic switching (super)current
density is three orders of magnitude less than that in a ferromagnetic metal with SOC.
These observations suggest an emergent ferromagnetic impurity state in a Rashba superconductor,
which can be controlled by applying supercurrents.

## Introduction

One of the immediate challenges facing high-speed computation using superconductors is a lack of fast
cryogenic memory with low drive power [1]. Non-superconducting memories widely used nowadays
are too slow and power-demanding for single-flux quantum electronics [2]. Superconducting memories
based on Josephson junctions [3,4] provide a faster solution but suffer from vortex trapping and
scalability problem [5]. A magnetic superconductor which can be switched by a supercurrent may be a
candidate material to overcome these current limitations. However, extrinsic ferromagnetic moments
breaks Cooper pairs in s-wave superconductors and supercurrent exerts Lorentz force on free vortices,
causing energy dissipation.

Utilizing supercurrent to mediate ferromagnetism among local magnetic moments may overcome these
problems. In normal metals, charge carriers ena ble magnetic coupling among magnetic impurities
through the Ruderman-Kittel-Kasuya-Yosida (RKKY) interaction [6–8]. Superconductors have a
quasiparticle gap and therefore the RKCKY mechanism between impurities is exponentially suppressed.
However, in superconductors with RIashba SOC, non-exponential decaying interaction between
magnetic impurities has been predicted [9] from a RKKY-like calculation of the spin-spin correlation
function. A later work, wiAth a complete analysis of such magnetic coupling, which includes the London-
Pearl screening effects, showed that the interaction of the anomalous supercurrents stemming from
different impurities can mediate a long-range ferromagnetic coupling [10]. This prediction opens up the
possibility of electric controlling of the magnetic state of a system of magnetic impurities in a
superconductor, a situation we explore in the present work.

The detection of current-induced magnetization in magnetic heterostructures typically relies on Hall
resistance, which is regarded as proportional to the magnetization. Such a Hall response does not occur
in a superconductor due to the vanishing resistance [11]. Therefore, a technique directly sensitive to the
magnetic induction from the magnetization and anomalous supercurrents is essential for detecting long-
range magnetization in Rashba superconductors. In this manuscript, we use scanning superconducting
quantum interference device (sSQUID) microscopy [12–21] to image the long-range magnetization of
Rashba superconductor Fe(Se,Te) in the high interstitial Fe density regime.

Fe-chalcogenide superconductor Fe(Se,Te) has exhibited strong spin-orbit coupling, which leads to
superconducting topological surface states [31–35]. The excess Fe atoms occupy interstitial sites and act

spectroscopy [40] and nitrogen-vacancy center magnetometry [41]. However, the impurity moments
naturally break time-reversal symmetry locally and the establishment of a long-range ferromagnetic
order requires a suitable impurity density and effective means to align possible magnetic domains.

## Paper

## Abstract

Conventional superconductors disfavor ferromagnetism because the supercurrent-carrying
electrons are paired into anti-parallel spin singlets. Consequently, ferromagnetic coupling
between localized moments through the charge carriers is absent in s-wave superconductors.
However, Rashba-type spin-orbit coupling (SOC) can profoundly alter the interaction between
the charge carriers and localized spins. Here, we report long-range ferromagnetic order among
the impurity moments on the surface of an s-wave SOC superconductor, Fe(Se,Te). We employ
scanning superconducting quantum interference device microscopy and find suppressed vortex
states but spontaneous magnetic domains in the superconducting state. Homogeneous remanent
flux patterns are induced by applying supercurrents through the sample. The patterns are
consistent with anomalous edge and bulk supercurrents generated by long-range in-plane
magnetization related to the magneto-electric effect intrinsic to a Rashba superconductor. The
anomalous supercurrents occur above a bias current threshold and follow hysteresis loops
reminiscent of those of a ferromagnet. Surprisingly, the magnetic switching (super)current
density is three orders of magnitude less than that in a ferromagnetic metal with SOC.
These observations suggest an emergent ferromagnetic impurity state in a Rashba superconductor,
which can be controlled by applying supercurrents.

---

## Introduction

One of the immediate challenges facing high-speed computation using superconductors is a lack of fast
cryogenic memory with low drive power [1]. Non-superconducting memories widely used nowadays
are too slow and power-demanding for single-flux quantum electronics [2]. Superconducting memories
based on Josephson junctions [3,4] provide a faster solution but suffer from vortex trapping and
scalability problem [5]. A magnetic superconductor which can be switched by a supercurrent may be a
candidate material to overcome these current limitations. However, extrinsic ferromagnetic moments
breaks Cooper pairs in s-wave superconductors and supercurrent exerts Lorentz force on free vortices,
causing energy dissipation.

Utilizing supercurrent to mediate ferromagnetism among local magnetic moments may overcome these
problems. In normal metals, charge carriers ena ble magnetic coupling among magnetic impurities
through the Ruderman-Kittel-Kasuya-Yosida (RKKY) interaction [6–8]. Superconductors have a
quasiparticle gap and therefore the RKCKY mechanism between impurities is exponentially suppressed.
However, in superconductors with RIashba SOC, non-exponential decaying interaction between
magnetic impurities has been predicted [9] from a RKKY-like calculation of the spin-spin correlation
function. A later work, wiAth a complete analysis of such magnetic coupling, which includes the London-
Pearl screening effects, showed that the interaction of the anomalous supercurrents stemming from
different impurities can mediate a long-range ferromagnetic coupling [10]. This prediction opens up the
possibility of electric controlling of the magnetic state of a system of magnetic impurities in a
superconductor, a situation we explore in the present work.

The detection of current-induced magnetization in magnetic heterostructures typically relies on Hall
resistance, which is regarded as proportional to the magnetization. Such a Hall response does not occur
in a superconductor due to the vanishing resistance [11]. Therefore, a technique directly sensitive to the
magnetic induction from the magnetization and anomalous supercurrents is essential for detecting long-
range magnetization in Rashba superconductors. In this manuscript, we use scanning superconducting
quantum interference device (sSQUID) microscopy [12–21] to image the long-range magnetization of
Rashba superconductor Fe(Se,Te) in the high interstitial Fe density regime.

---

## Results

Observation of spontaneous magnetic domains in superconducting Fe(Se,Te) with interstitial
magnetic impurity
To comprehend the emergence of such ferromagnetic ordering, we briefly revisit the key aspects of the
theory. In Rashba superconductors and in superconductors with surfaces supporting a Dirac band, the
symmetry allows for a term in the Ginzburg-Landau free energy of the form of Lifshitz invariant 𝐹 =
𝜅(𝐧×𝐁)∙ℏ∇𝜑 [22–24], where ∇𝜑 is a phase gradient in the order parameter, 𝐁 is the magnetic
induction, 𝐧 is the surface normal, and 𝜅 is the Edelstein constant, which depends on the Rashba
splitting of the Kramer’s pair at the Fermi level. For Dirac surface states, it is a limiting case of a large
Rashba SOC when the physics is dominated by only one helical band. A direct consequence of the
Lifshitz invariant is that any supercurrent 𝐉 (being proportional to ∇𝜑) induces polarization of surface
impurity moments, which has been observed on isolated quantum anoSmalous vortex and antivortex in
Fe(Se,Te) (Fig. 1a) [25].

The inverse effect, in analogy with the spin-galvanic effect in SOC metals, is that a local magnetic
moment polarizes the condensate and generates anoma lous supercurrents 𝐉
𝐚
∝ 𝐧×𝐒 at the center of
the impurity moment 𝐒 [9,26–28]. Surrounding the impurity, 𝐉 follows a dipolar distribution that
𝐚
decays as a power law and extends over lonEg distances away from the magnetic impurity (Fig. 1b) [10].
Confined to the surface plane, two impurity spins favor an alignment along their center line (Fig. 1c).
Such a configuration minimizes the total supercurrent on both impurities and thus reduces the free
energy. For disordered impurity Tspins on a plane, ferromagnetic coupling leads to long-range in-plane
magnetization 𝐌 which generates an edge 𝐉 with an opposite flow direction from that in the bulk
𝐉 𝐚
(Fig. 1d) [23]. With the exception of square lattices where anti-ferromagnetism is favored [10], Rashba
SOC allows the interesting possibility that a ferromagnetic order in a system of magnetic impurities can
be established via coupling to the superconducting condensate. Indeed, the ferromagnetic order is the
one that minimized the energy of the anomalous currents induced by the magnetoelectric effect due to
the SOC around each impurity.

Just like in a ferromagnet, where an external magnetic field is necessary to align magnetic domains, a
uniform magnetization across the sample is facilitated by applying a global supercurrent. In magnetic
heterostructures with Rashba SOC, the magnetization follows hysteretic switching under external
current [29,30]. The magnetic effect of an external supercurrent on a Rashba or Dirac superconductor
with magnetic impurities has yet to be experimentally studied. In general, in the absence of a constant
bias current or external magnetic field, both magnetization and anomalous supercurrents produce
magnetic induction, the spatial distribution of which depends on sample geometry. Measuring such a
magnetic signal and its evolution after applying a current may provide key evidence for the
supercurrent-mediated long-range ferromagnetic coupling of magnetic impurities.

Fe-chalcogenide superconductor Fe(Se,Te) has exhibited strong spin-orbit coupling, which leads to
superconducting topological surface states [31–35]. The excess Fe atoms occupy interstitial sites and act
as magnetic impurities [36]. Their interaction with the superconducting condensate enables phenomena
such as the quantum anomalous vortex state [25]. Scanning tunneling microscopy studies have found
zero-energy bound states in vortex cores or interstitial Fe sites on its surface [33,37–39]. Signs of time-
reversal symmetry breaking have also been reported on the surface states from photoemission
spectroscopy [40] and nitrogen-vacancy center magnetometry [41]. However, the impurity moments

Response to Reviewer #2
Xiang et al. report on a scanning SQUID study of flakes of Fe(Se,Te) with relatively high
Fe density. The main observation is flux patterns that change in a hysteretic way after
applying a current bias through the flakes. A comprehensive study of this behavior is
presented, including an analysis of magnetic field training through Meissner currents. Data
from three flakes are shown. The remnant flux is attributed to magnetization induced by a
RKKY-like interaction, enabled in the superconducting state by strong SOC. This would be
an interesting demonstration of the interplay between magnetic impurities and
superconductivity.
-We thank the reviewer for the careful reading and high evaluation of our manuscript.
We also appreciate the constructive suggestions and the opportunity to improve it.
However, there are several major issues with the interpretation of the data, which I describe
below. These problems preclude me from recommending publication at this point.
Most importantly, the authors do not properly account for the inhomogeneity of the samples,
which I believe is sufficient to explain the observations. The susceptibility of all the flakes
in this study is highly inhomogeneous. For example the top part of the flake in Fig. 3 does
not appear to be superconducting even at the base temperature. This means the critical
current is different for different regions in the sample. The change to the current distribution,
and the remnant magnetization, are correlated with the top part of that flake turning normal.
This motivates the following interpretation: once the critical current for the top part is
reached, the current flows through the edges of the bottom part, generating a magnetic
field through the flake. When the current is gradually removed, the top part turns
superconducting in the presence of this field. This results in Meissner currents and/or
vortices, and because the Pearl length is so large, they manifest as a “homogeneous”
flux signal.
The other data shown are consistent with this alternative interpretation, for example the
remnant flux pattern in extended data 11 is correlated with the superfluid density landscape,
rather than with current density pattern that would be generated in this geometry.
To exclude this explanation, I suggest the authors either repeat the experiment on a single
crystal sample, or on more homogeneous flakes, and provide a better characterization of
the local critical temperature and current density distributions in the existing data.
- We thank the reviewer for bringing up an alternative interpretation of our findings. We
acknowledge the inhomogeneity of the samples, which arises from the stochastic
distribution of interstitial iron atoms. However, our data is not consistent with the
vortex
trapping scenario, as we elucidate below.
1. In Extended Data Figures 8b and e, we use two electrodes on the bottom edge of the
sample so that the bias current favors to flow along the bottom edge. This current
configuration generates a positive magnetic field within the sample. However, we
observed remanent flux signal with a negative polarity (Extended Data Figures 8b),
which contradicts the vortex trapping scenario. The same argument also applies to the
remnant flux pattern depicted in Extended Data Figure 8c, which is more consistent
with the anomalous supercurrent picture we propose [Phys. Rev. B 102, 060506, (2020);
Phys. Rev. B 108, L180506 (2023)].
2. We have expanded the image range of sample #2 in Extended Data Figures 4 and 7.
We can see that the superfluid density on the left part of the flake is depleted at I = 200
b
μA. Hence, this region would be expected to be more susceptible to vortex trapping.
However, this region shows negligibly small remnant flux.
3. Our observation of the sudden onset of edge current above some threshold does not
agree with vortex trapping. From Extended Data Figures 4d, we can see that the
diamagnetism of the sample at I = 200 μA is still present on the bottom edge, which is
b
the region where the edge current shows a strong contrast (Fig. 3).
4. The temperature dependence of the remnant flux (Fig. 4f) provides additional
evidence against vortex penetration. The variation of integrated magnetic flux with
increasing temperature is much smaller than the flux quantum, which is inconsistent
with leakage of vortices with increasing temperature.
5. We have repeated the experiment on a more homogeneous flake sample (Extended
Data Figure 12). We have observed the spontaneous magnetic domains (Extended Data
Figure 12b) as well as the alignment of domains by a bias current (Extended Data
Figures 12c and d). In this sample, the switching current is about 1.6 mA (Extended
Data Figure 12f) which is far below the critical current of 6 mA (Extended Data Figure
12e), making the possibility of vortex trapping highly unlikely. Furthermore, the sign
of the remanent flux is consistent with that on samples #1 and #2 and opposite from the
Biot-Savart field of the current.
We have added these discussions to Lines 216-221 and Lines 304-311 in the revised
manuscript.
